questions.prompt: The original reverseLetters accepts ASCII text a-B!c. Which contract applies?

options.label: Reverse only ASCII letters and keep every other accepted ASCII character at its original position.
Reverse all code points, including punctuation and digits.
Normalize every language into ASCII before reversing, without rejecting input.

questions.explanation: The result is c-B!a: only ASCII letters move, and punctuation stays at its index. Reversing all characters changes the fixed-position contract. Non-ASCII input is rejected; normalization and grapheme rules belong to a separate exercise.

questions.prompt: What ensures the two-pointer reversal loop cannot stall on punctuation?

options.label: Advance at least one pointer each iteration; skip fixed characters and move both pointers after a swap.
Only advance pointers when both ends contain letters, leaving other iterations unchanged.
Delete punctuation first, then insert it at arbitrary positions after reversal.

questions.explanation: Each branch progresses: skip a fixed left or right character, or swap and move both. Failing to advance on punctuation can loop forever. Removing and arbitrarily reinserting punctuation loses the specified original positions.

questions.prompt: A regex finds a substring in a candidate token. What must a whole-input validator still check?

options.label: Use the intended dialect and verify the matched text covers the entire input.
Any nonempty substring match makes the entire input valid.
An end assertion has identical meaning for every dialect and flag set.

questions.explanation: Matching a substring does not validate the remaining characters. State dialect, flags and API, then check complete coverage and rejected boundaries. End assertions and multiline behavior vary; an engine diagram is not a portable full-match contract.

questions.prompt: How does a RegExp constructor string differ from a regex literal?

options.label: A constructor string needs the JavaScript escape layer before the regex parser receives the pattern.
The constructor always removes the need to escape regex syntax.
A visualizer guarantees that a single backslash survives every string parser unchanged.

questions.explanation: A constructor first receives a parsed JavaScript string, so a backslash intended for the regex must survive that layer. A literal has different source syntax. Neither a constructor nor a diagram removes the underlying regex escape rules.

questions.prompt: A regex diagram looks correct. What evidence does that provide?

options.label: A diagram helps explain structure; it proves neither dialect equivalence nor bounded runtime.
It proves the pattern runs in linear time on every engine and input.
It grants permission to send private source text to the external tool.

questions.explanation: Visualization can aid review of grouping and repetition. Engine behavior and adversarial runtime need separate checks. A useful interface does not establish authorization to disclose private text; the original fixture uses synthetic local inputs.
